Chai Ice Cream

ByAlyssa Adams Posted onSeptember 30, 2026October 13, 2026

This post may contain affiliate links.

Jump to Recipe Jump to Video Jump to Comments

Instaread

If there’s one thing I love more than chai spices, it’s chai spices with a little caramel. When done right (because it can easily be overdone!), the toasted sugar intensifies the flavor of the cinnamon, cardamom, and ginger without being cloying. It’s my favorite way to sweeten chai-spiced desserts, so it was only fair that I add a caramel swirl to this homemade chai ice cream. Store-bought caramel sauce is usually on the thinner side, so I tend to make my own with a dry technique to get thick and gooey caramel ribbons.

For the ice cream base, I used my favorite brown sugar custard recipe with chai spices, similar to my cinnamon graham ice cream. Then, I steeped two teaspoons of black tea in the custard overnight as it chilled. That’s the trick to get a deeply chai-flavored custard that’s just like a chai latte in ice cream form. The chai base on its own isn’t too sweet, which makes it the ideal vessel for that caramel swirl. But even with caramel ribbons, it’s balanced among all the spices—and you can still taste the notes of black tea!

If you’d like to add some mix-ins, like pieces of snickerdoodles or chai cookies, you can comfortably add about half a cup in the last few minutes of churning, or layer them in by hand with the caramel swirl.

Ingredients for Chai Ice Cream

This homemade chai ice cream recipe is made with standard custard ingredients, plus chai spices and tea. I specifically used ground spices when developing this recipe, since they’re a lot cheaper and easier to find (and it doesn’t have to feel like a special occasion to use whole spices). The full recipe is at the bottom of the post, but I’ve listed what each ingredient does and substitutions where possible below:

  • Brown sugar. The hint of molasses in brown sugar complements the warm chai spices really nicely. The sucrose in the brown sugar lowers the freezing point for a smooth, scoopable ice cream.
  • Heavy cream. The fat in heavy cream is essential to give us creamy frozen custard with a perfectly scoopable consistency.
  • Whole milk. This is the place for indulgence—whole milk contains enough fat to make ice cream creamy. Using lower fat milk will result in icier ice cream.
  • Chai spices. I use a mix of cinnamon, cardamom, nutmeg, ginger, and cloves. A couple turns of fresh black pepper could also work nicely for a little heat!
  • Egg yolks. Yolks contain emulsifiers that help stabilize the ice cream base with a classic custard flavor.
  • Chai-spiced tea. Infusing the custard with real tea adds flavor that you can’t get from spices alone. If you don’t want the caffeine in your evening scoop (I understand!), I recommend using a decaffeinated or herbal chai instead.
  • Vanilla bean paste or extract. I like to use a little vanilla bean paste for additional warmth. Vanilla extract works, too.
  • Salt. Just a pinch helps to enhance flavor and balance sweetness.
  • Salted caramel sauce (optional). Caramel is an optional mix-in, but it complements the spices nicely. I made my salted caramel sauce recipe as written for this photoshoot, just without the water.
  • Other mix-ins (optional). I kept the base recipe fairly simple to allow you to add your own mix-ins, like pieces of chai cookies, snickerdoodles, or vanilla shortbread.

My Favorite Equipment for Making Homemade Ice Cream

You will need to use an ice cream maker or similar for velvety smooth frozen custard. I use Cuisinart’s 1.5-quart ice cream maker, but you can also use the KitchenAid ice cream bowl or a fancier compressor model. It’s also possible to make this chai ice cream recipe in the Ninja Creami or Cuisinart FastFreeze, but I prefer the texture when traditionally churned.

I like to store my ice cream in long, reusable ice cream containers with silicone seals. The seal keeps the ice cream fresh, and the length makes it easy to get picture-perfect scoops of ice cream for cones and bowls. And, as a bonus, these ones come with stickers to label your ice cream!

If you don’t already have an ice cream scoop you like, my husband found this stainless steel ice cream scoop last year, and it became our favorite.

Quick Tips to Make Chai Frozen Custard

Even if you’re new to making custard-based ice cream, you’re in good hands!

The following sections will provide an overview of how to make homemade chai-spiced ice cream so that you know what to expect for every step. If you’re new to ice cream making, I recommend at least skimming these instructions and photos so you know what to look for.

Make the Chai Custard Base

First, dry toast the ground spices in a medium pot over medium heat for a minute or two until fragrant to release some of the essential oils. This gives you a stronger flavor without having to use more ground spices, which sometimes gets gritty.

Then, add half of the brown sugar, heavy cream, and whole milk (in that order—the milk may scald if added first) to the pot and stir to combine. Warm the mixture, stirring occasionally, until it’s just about steaming but not yet boiling.

As the milk mixture heats up, whisk together egg yolks and the remaining brown sugar in a large, heat-safe bowl. The mixture will be a dark yellow-brown at the start, but it will get lighter as you whisk more air into the batter. Using a large balloon whisk helps the mixture aerate more quickly, too! After about two minutes of whisking, the mixture should be much lighter in color and airy.

If you are new to tempering eggs, I recommend whisking the eggs for another minute or two beyond that, to the ribbon stage. This incorporates more air into the mixture, which better insulates the eggs and makes the batter more resistant to curdling.

Tempering the Egg Yolks

Next, slowly stream the warm chai cream into the ribboned yolks a few Tablespoons at a time, whisking constantly. When that cream has been fully incorporated, add another splash and stir until combined.

Repeat this process until you’ve added about half of the chai cream to the yolk mixture. Then, pour the tempered yolk mixture back into the pot with the rest of the chai-spiced cream. Scrape the bowl with your spatula to remove any spices or liquid left behind, and return the pot to medium heat. Cook the chai custard to 165°F/74°C to finish cooking, which will thicken the base.

Chilling the Chai Custard

Once fully cooked, transfer the chai custard into a heat-safe bowl. I always reuse the same bowl, as the mixture is hot enough to cook any dredges that got left behind. You’re welcome to use a new bowl if you prefer.

Add your tea (either bagged or loose leaf) and vanilla to the custard, then stir to combine. Cover and place in the fridge to chill until cold to the touch, usually at least four hours. You can speed this process up by using an ice bath, but I like the depth of flavor you get from a long, overnight steep.

How to Churn Homemade Chai Ice Cream

Right before churning the chai ice cream base, place the ice cream container you plan to use in the freezer. This will prevent the ice cream from melting directly upon contact when you transfer it out of the ice cream maker later!

If using loose leaf tea, strain the mix in advance. For individual sachets, remove the bags. In both cases, extract all of the flavor by squeezing any excess custard out of the tea. Then, pour the custard into your ice cream maker. Churn according to the manufacturer’s instructions, until the ice cream forms rounded domes over the paddle. It usually takes my ice cream maker around 20 minutes for this batch to churn completely.

In the last couple minutes of churning, take your container and any mix-ins out of the fridge/freezer. I like to heat up my salted caramel sauce in the microwave for about 20 seconds to make it more pliable, then I transfer it to a piping bag for easy portioning.

Get Scoopable Ice Cream Every Time

To prevent your ice cream from freezing quite as hard, you may want to increase the overrun. Overrun, in regards to ice cream, is the amount of air you churn into the custard while it’s freezing. Rather than going by time (as manufacturers often suggest), try going by look and feel instead. I always churn my ice creams until I see large, rounded domes above the paddle of my ice cream maker. This signals that the ice cream is sufficiently frozen and churned, so it won’t melt quite as quickly upon transfer. See the image below for an example.

How to Add a Caramel Swirl to Homemade Ice Cream

Use a heavy-duty spatula to transfer about a third of the ice cream into your ice cream container. Add a layer of salted caramel across the entire top. A piping bag works really well to contain the mess (especially with something as sticky as caramel!), but you can also use a spoon, if you like.

Top with another layer of ice cream, then add another few lines of caramel on top. Repeat one or two more times, depending on how much ice cream is left. You should have 3-4 layers of ice cream with salted caramel ribbons between each one! If desired, use a spoon to swirl the caramel into ripples.

Other Recipes You May Enjoy

This is the third recipe of my 2026 chai series, following my chai cookies and chai granola. I hope you’ve been enjoying eating your chai and drinking it, too!

Ever since I made caramel chai muffins in 2021, it’s been one of my favorite fall flavor combinations. I even recommend adding a caramel center to my chai macarons in the recipe card.

Dish Cleanup: Gonna Take a While

I rate my recipe cleanups on a scale of 1 to 5. 1 is only a handful of dishes, and 5 is everything including the kitchen sink.

This frozen chai custard has a cleanup rating of a 4. There’s the pot to make the custard, the ice cream maker bowl, the paddle, and a handful of measuring cups and spoons. However, there are no cutting boards, knives, or food processors, which makes this an easier cleanup than most of my other ice cream recipes. (I’d even reduce it to a 3 if the ice cream bowl wasn’t as much of a pain to clean.)

Chai Ice Cream with a Caramel Swirl

Author: Alyssa Adams of The Floral Apron
Developed to taste just like a chai latte, this custard-based chai ice cream is infused with both chai spices and black tea for maximum flavor. Add an optional swirl of caramel for even more depth without being too sweet.
Print Recipe Pin Recipe
Prep Time:25 minutes mins
Cook Time:20 minutes mins
Chill Time:8 hours hrs
Total Time:8 hours hrs 45 minutes mins
Course: Ice Creams
Cuisine: American
Servings: 8 about 1.5 quarts

Ingredients
 

For the Chai-Spiced Ice Cream

  • ¾ cup (160 g) brown sugar packed
  • 1 ½ cups (350 ml) heavy cream
  • 1 ½ cups (350 ml) whole milk
  • ¾ teaspoon ground cardamom
  • ¾ teaspoon ground cinnamon
  • ½ teaspoon ground nutmeg
  • ½ teaspoon ground ginger
  • 1 pinch ground cloves
  • 4 large egg yolks
  • 2-3 teaspoons or bags chai-spiced tea*
  • 1 teaspoon vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract
  • 1 pinch of salt

For the Caramel Swirl (optional)

  • ¼-⅓ cup (80-100 g) salted caramel sauce store-bought or homemade**

Instructions

Making the Brown Sugar Chai Custard Base

  1. In a medium pot over medium heat, toast the spices over medium heat for 1-2 minutes until fragrant.
    ¾ teaspoon ground cardamom, ¾ teaspoon ground cinnamon, ½ teaspoon ground nutmeg, ½ teaspoon ground ginger, 1 pinch ground cloves
  2. Add half of the brown sugar (about ⅓ cup or 80 g), heavy cream, whole milk, and a pinch of salt. Stir occasionally for 8-10 minutes, until the cream mixture is warm and steamy. Some of the spices will float at the top rather than incorporating; that's okay.
    ¾ cup (160 g) brown sugar, 1 ½ cups (350 ml) heavy cream, 1 ½ cups (350 ml) whole milk, 1 pinch of salt
  3. Meanwhile, whisk together four yolks and the remaining half of the brown sugar in a large heat-safe bowl. Whisk for about a minute until the yolk mixture thickens to the ribbon stage (where the mixture falls off the whisk in ribbons that are clearly visible on the top of the batter before disappearing back into the mixture).
    4 large egg yolks

Tempering the Egg Yolks

  1. Remove the warm cream mixture from heat and carefully pour about 1-2 Tablespoons (15-30 ml) into the yolk mixture at a time, whisking vigorously until incorporated. Repeat 1-2 Tablespoons (15-30 ml) at a time until you've added about half of the cream mixture.
  2. Pour the egg yolk mixture back into the pot with the cream mixture and return to medium heat. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the custard is thick enough to coat the back of a spoon or reaches 170°F/75°C, about 5-10 minutes. Do not let the custard boil.***
  3. Pour the custard into a large heat-safe bowl. (I always use the same one the egg yolk mixture was in, but you're welcome to use a clean bowl.)
  4. Stir in the vanilla bean paste or extract and add the tea (loose leaf or bagged) to steep while it cools. Cover the bowl and chill in the fridge for at least four hours or up to one day, until the mixture is cold to the touch.
    1 teaspoon vanilla bean paste, 2-3 teaspoons or bags chai-spiced tea*

Churning the Chai Custard

  1. Place the container in which you'll store the ice cream in the freezer, along with any mix-ins you plan to use. Remove the tea bags or strain the tea from the custard base with a fine mesh strainer.
  2. Once chilled, pour the custard into a ice cream maker and churn according to manufacturer's instructions, until the ice cream forms rounded domes over the paddle. This usually takes around 20 minutes.
    In the last few minutes of churning, heat up the caramel sauce to a pourable consistency and transfer to a piping bag for easy layering, if using.
  3. Transfer the chai-spiced ice cream to your chilled container in stages: Layer about a third of the ice cream on the bottom of the container, then pipe a couple rows of salted caramel sauce on top. Add another layer of ice cream, followed by another few rows of caramel. Add the remaining ice cream, then top with another few rows of caramel. To swirl the ice cream, run a spoon or knife side to side and up and down the length of the container.
    ¼-⅓ cup (80-100 g) salted caramel sauce
  4. For caramel chai soft serve, enjoy right away (though the warm caramel may make it a bit melty!).
    For traditional brown sugar chai ice cream, cover and freeze for at least six hours or preferably overnight to allow the ice cream to firm up before serving.

Notes

*Infusing the base with chai tea adds a depth of flavor you can’t get with just chai spices alone. If you’re sensitive to caffeine, you can substitute a decaffeinated or herbal chai-spiced tea, like rooibos—or omit the tea entirely for a good (but slightly less full!) flavor.
**I made my existing caramel sauce recipe more ice cream friendly by omitting the water. That gives you a thicker sauce that freezes less hard.
***If the custard boils, the egg yolks may curdle. However, if it happens, it’s recoverable: Simply pass the ice cream through a fine mesh strainer to catch any lumps before chilling.
This ice cream will have the best flavor and texture when eaten within 1-2 weeks. Store in the freezer in an airtight container for up to three months.

Recommended Supplies

  • Cuisinart Ice Cream Maker Machine, 1.5 Quart Sorbet, Frozen Yogurt Maker, Double Insulated, White, ICE-21P1
  • Set of 2 Reusable Ice Cream Tub Containers For Homemade Ice Cream 1.6 Quart – Stackable Storage Containers, Stickers, And Lids
  • Mason Cash Batter Bowl
  • Cuisinart Silicone Whisk, 10-Inch, Black
  • OXO Stainless Steel Ice Cream Scoop

FAQs about Caramel Chai Ice Cream

Sugar plays an invaluable role in lowering the freezing temperature of the custard base. I don’t recommend reducing the sugar, as it will cause the custard to freeze much harder and be more difficult to scoop. You can omit the salted caramel sauce without any issues, though!

I recommend any butter-based cookie, like snickerdoodles, these chai cookies, or even vanilla shortbread. Freeze them for at least two hours before churning your ice cream to prevent them from losing all their crispiness.

You can, if you’d like. Steeping the tea adds a distinct “tea” flavor, but it’s still recognizable as chai ice cream without the tea. You can also substitute a decaf or herbal chai!
